title: Grace perfects nature
hook: Aquinas: grace doesn't destroy what's human but completes it

segments.voice: Yesterday, the five ways: Aquinas following a moving world back to a first mover. Your line was everything moves. What did you see change, and did you ask what moved it? Day one thousand two hundred fifty-one.

A wedding in a village called Cana, and in the middle of the feast the wine runs out. Jesus tells the servants to fill the stone jars with water and take some to the man running the feast. He tastes it, and it's wine, and he calls the groom over, puzzled: "thou hast kept the good wine until now." Notice what Jesus didn't do. He didn't cancel the party. He didn't replace the wedding with a prayer meeting. He took plain water, the stuff of an ordinary day, and made it better than anyone expected. Thomas Aquinas has a short line that fits that pattern.

Near the start of his Summa, Aquinas is asking whether reason has any place in sacred teaching. His answer turns on a short phrase: grace does not destroy nature, but perfects it. Grace here means God's own gift, given freely. Nature means what we are as creatures: bodies, minds, appetites, friendships, the ability to think. Aquinas's point is that God's gift doesn't come to wipe all that out and start over. It comes to finish it. So reason isn't faith's enemy; it can serve faith. And the same pattern runs through his whole picture of a human life. Courage, fairness, self-control: those are good human strengths, and grace doesn't cancel them. It lifts them toward faith, hope and love. Paul's letter to Timothy points the same way: "every creature of God is good, and nothing to be refused, if it be received with thanksgiving." Christians weigh this differently. Catholic teaching draws on Aquinas's line. Lutheran and Reformed teaching stresses how deeply sin has wounded human nature, so that grace must heal before it can complete. Orthodox Christians speak of human beings being drawn into God's own life. Aquinas also says grace heals a nature wounded by sin, but his emphasis falls on completion. In his picture, grace doesn't take a person out of being human. It finishes the work.

Here's the practice: enjoy one natural good. Settle, and breathe. Choose something ordinary and good that's within reach: the taste of what you're drinking, sunlight on your hands, a song you love, the warmth of a blanket. Give it your full attention. Don't hurry past it to something more spiritual. Let it be good. If you pray, you can receive it with thanksgiving, the way Paul's letter puts it. If you don't, simply let yourself enjoy it. The bell holds the time.
Grace perfects nature. Aquinas's line: God's gift doesn't destroy what's human, but completes it, the way water at Cana became good wine.
Your line: grace completes. Today, do one ordinary thing you're good at, cooking, fixing, listening, and do it as well as you can, as a gift. Day one thousand two hundred fifty-one.

howItsDone: Catholic teaching quotes Aquinas's line that grace perfects nature; Christians of different churches give thanks for food, work, friendship and beauty as good gifts of God.

notes: Aquinas paraphrased: 'since grace does not destroy nature but perfects it, natural reason should minister to faith' (I q.1 a.8 ad 2). The Latin in the original game is the usual short form; confirm wording.
Natural virtues lifted by the theological virtues summarizes Aquinas's teaching on infused virtue (I-II qq. 62–63); not cited separately.
Church differences: Lutheran/Reformed emphasis on sin's wounding of nature; Orthodox theosis described as 'being drawn into God's own life'. Check fairness; no ranking intended.

Editor pass: cut Genesis 1:31 ('very good'), which day 1238 quoted for the same point; cut 'often' and 'tend to' frequency claims and the unsupported 'none of them say creation is bad'; the closing line is now framed as Aquinas's picture ('in his picture, grace ... finishes the work') rather than the narrator's claim, and no longer echoes day 1246's 'human all the way down'.
Original pronunciation in classical-leaning style; ecclesiastical would be GRAH-tsee-ah ... PER-fee-chit.

Audit (2026-10-02): the church-differences passage made Aquinas look as if he ignored sin's wound, set against Lutheran and Reformed teaching; Aquinas also teaches healing grace (I-II q.109 a.2), now said. Hook no longer implies Aquinas drew his line from Cana. Pronunciation made consistently ecclesiastical.
